title: What are the rules for 1099 employees?
summary: What are the rules for 1099 employees? Forms, thresholds and the limits on control, explained. Start paying your contractors abroad with Grey today.
body_markdown:
The short answer is in the next paragraph, but the rest of this guide covers the details, from the forms you need to the limits on how much control you can have.


A 1099 worker is an independent contractor, not an employee, so most employment rules do not apply. You do not withhold payroll tax, but you should collect a Form W-9, file a 1099-NEC if you pay a US contractor $2,000 or more in a year, and avoid controlling how they work. Misclassifying workers carries penalties.


## Are 1099 workers really employees?


No. A 1099 worker is an independent contractor, not an employee. “1099 employee” is a popular shortcut, but it blends two different legal relationships, and the difference decides almost every rule in this guide.


The name comes from the form. Businesses report what they pay contractors on Form 1099-NEC, while employees receive a W-2. That one difference reflects a bigger one. An employee works for your business under your direction, and you withhold income and payroll taxes from their pay. A contractor runs their own business, decides how the work gets done, and pays their own taxes, including self-employment tax.


Employee 1099 contractor


Year-end form W-2 1099-NEC, if payments pass the threshold


Tax withholding You withhold income tax and payroll taxes You do not withhold (backup withholding aside)


Benefits Eligible for employer benefits Not eligible as a contractor


Control You direct how, when, and where the work is done They decide how the work is done


Taxes on their earnings Employer and employee share payroll taxes Contractor pays self-employment tax and estimated tax


The label in your contract does not settle the question. The IRS looks at the real working relationship, not just the title on the page, so a person you treat like staff can still be an employee even if you call them a contractor. If you want the full definition, read our guide to[what a 1099 employee is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099-employee) . A “1099 job” is simply work performed under this type of contractor arrangement.


The rules below apply to US tax law. If you hire people in other countries, local employment rules may also apply.


## The rules for engaging a 1099 contractor


Engaging a 1099 contractor comes down to six rules: confirm the work is genuinely independent, put the terms in writing, collect tax details before you pay, pay against invoices, keep records, and report the payments after the year ends. Use this checklist before the first payment goes out.


1. **Confirm the work is genuinely independent:** The contractor should control how the work is done, use their own tools, and be free to work for other clients. If you would need to train, schedule, and supervise them like staff, you are probably hiring an employee.
2. **Put the terms in writing:** A contract should cover scope, deliverables, deadlines, fees, payment terms, ownership of the finished work, confidentiality, and how either party can terminate the arrangement. State that the contractor is responsible for their own taxes, insurance, and equipment. A contract shows intent, but it does not decide classification on its own.
3. **Collect a Form W-9 before the first payment:** It provides the contractor’s legal name, address, and taxpayer identification number (TIN). Keep it on file. The IRS advises keeping it for four years.
4. **Pay against invoices:** The contractor invoices you for the work, and you pay the agreed amount in full on the agreed date, with no payroll deductions.
5. **Keep clear records:** Note the date, amount, and invoice number of every payment during the calendar year, because you will need the total when it is time to report.
6. **Report what you paid:** If you pay a contractor above the reporting threshold, file Form 1099-NEC and send the contractor a copy by 31 January of the following year.


Contractors based outside the US work differently. A foreign contractor cannot complete a W-9, which is for US persons. They provide a Form W-8BEN (for individuals) or W-8BEN-E (for entities) instead, and the IRS says that a valid W-8 generally exempts the payee from backup withholding and from Form 1099 reporting. Whether any other US tax rules apply can depend on where the work is performed, so check with a tax professional before you pay someone abroad.


## Forms and thresholds


Two forms matter for most small businesses: Form W-9, which the contractor completes, and Form 1099-NEC, which you file.


**Form W-9**
The contractor fills in their name, business name (if applicable), tax classification, address, and TIN (a Social Security number or an employer identification number), then signs it. You keep the form in your records. You do not send it to the IRS. Ask for it before the first payment, because if a US contractor does not provide a TIN, you generally have to apply a 24% backup withholding to what you pay them.


o pay themThe[IRS instructions for requesters of Form W-9](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/iw9) confirm that rate and say it applies straight away to nonemployee compensation. If you do backup withholding, you report it on Form 945.


**Form 1099-NEC**
NEC stands for nonemployee compensation, which is what you pay a contractor for services. You report the total you paid each contractor during the calendar year, not each individual payment. The reporting threshold has changed recently:


- **Payments made in 2025:** $600 or more.
- **Payments made after 31 December 2025:** $2,000 or more, which may be adjusted for inflation from 2027.


That means payments you make during 2026 are reported in January 2027, and the $2,000 threshold applies. The[IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1099mec.pdf) set out the current figures and are worth checking each year.


The deadline is 31 January. You send one copy to the IRS and one to the contractor, and if that date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day. 31 January 2027 is a Sunday, so the deadline will move to Monday, 1 February. If you file 10 or more information returns in a year, you must file them electronically.


A few more points are worth knowing:


- Payments to corporations generally do not need a 1099-NEC, though attorneys’ fees are an exception.
- Late or missing filings can lead to penalties, and the amount increases the longer you wait.
- For a plain-English overview of the wider 1099 family, see[what a 1099 form is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099) .


*This is general guidance, not professional tax advice. Consult a certified tax professional for your specific situation.*


## What you cannot do


You cannot control how a 1099 contractor does the work, treat them like a member of staff, or offer them employee benefits as if they were one. Doing so puts the arrangement at risk of being reclassified as employment, regardless of what your contract says.


The IRS sorts the evidence into three groups, and no single factor decides the outcome:


- **Behavioural control.** Do you control, or have the right to control, what the worker does and how they do it? Setting their daily hours, dictating their methods, requiring training, or supervising their day-to-day work all point towards employment.
- **Financial control.** Do you control the business side of the job? Reimbursing expenses, supplying tools, and deciding how they are paid all matter. A contractor typically invoices, uses their own equipment, and can make a profit or a loss.
- **Type of relationship.** Is there a written contract, or are there employee-type benefits such as insurance, a pension plan, or paid leave? Is the relationship ongoing, and is the work a key part of your business?


The[IRS guidance on independent contractors and employees](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/independent-contractor-self-employed-or-employee) goes into detail on each group, and our guide to[contractor vs employee](https://grey.co/blog/contractor-vs-employee) shows how to tell the two apart in practice.


What you can do is agree on the result. You can set deadlines, deliverables, quality standards, and confidentiality terms. You can also end the contract if the work is not delivered. The line is between controlling the outcome, which is fine, and controlling the method, which is not.


Misclassification is the main risk. It means treating a worker as a contractor when the facts say they are an employee. If the IRS reclassifies them, you may owe employment taxes, plus penalties and interest, and state agencies may take their own action. If you are unsure, the IRS offers Form SS-8, which either you or the worker can file for an official determination, though it can take at least six months.


There is also the Voluntary Classification Settlement Program, which allows eligible businesses to reclassify workers as employees going forward and receive partial relief from federal employment taxes.

## Frequently asked questions about the rules for 1099 employees


### Is a 1099 worker an employee?


No. A 1099 worker is an independent contractor who runs their own business, pays their own taxes, and decides how the work gets done. Employees receive a W-2 and have taxes withheld from their pay.


### What forms do I need?


For a US contractor, you need a Form W-9 from them before you pay, and you file Form 1099-NEC if you pay them above the threshold. If you apply backup withholding, you also file Form 945. For an individual contractor based abroad, you generally collect a Form W-8BEN instead of a W-9.


### What is the 1099 threshold?


For payments made after 31 December 2025, the threshold for Form 1099-NEC is $2,000 in a calendar year. It was $600 for payments made in 2025, and it may be adjusted for inflation from 2027.


### Can I set their hours?


Generally, no. Setting a contractor’s daily hours is a sign of control and points to an employment relationship. You can agree on deadlines and delivery dates, but the contractor should decide when and how they work to meet them.


### What is misclassification?


Misclassification is treating someone as an independent contractor when the facts show they are an employee. It can lead to back employment taxes, penalties, and interest, so check the IRS tests before you engage anyone.
